title: ‘What Do You Need?’ Wednesday: All Talk
author: Episcopal Academy CTL
summary: This weekly teaching digest from Episcopal Academy's Center for Teaching and Learning is devoted to the idea that students need to think out loud. It curates three recent pieces and closes with a classic. The first is Zia Hassan's guest post at Grading for Growth on question-only peer coaching as a way to make AI-assisted writing less tempting by shifting focus from product to process. The second is Tom Sherrington's Teacherhead piece arguing that talking promotes attention, thinking, and retrieval, so everyone should practice it like lay-ups in basketball. The third is Mary Resanovich's NWEA blog on the five practices for orchestrating productive mathematics discussions. The last word is Heinrich von Kleist's essay on constructing thoughts during speech. Each item comes with a short Try this prompt teachers can use in class immediately.
points: Hassan's peer-coaching routine has students ask only questions, which shifts attention from the product to the process of writing.
Sherrington argues that talking is a way of thinking, so think-pair-share should involve every student rather than a handful.
Comparing how students explain the same lesson reveals where it landed and where to go next.
Resanovich's piece on the five practices centers on teachers deciding which student ideas to surface and in what order.
Kleist's essay supplies the closing idea that we often work out what we think by saying it aloud.
quotes: Ultimately, Hassan’s piece demonstrates one teacher’s attempt at shifting the focus from product to process, and it emphasizes that the act of talking is also a form of thinking.
If talking something through helps one student learn, why let only a handful of students do it?
The part that stuck with us most, though, is his observation that if you ask three people to explain a sunset (or D-Day, or Macbeth), you’ll get three different accounts, even after the same lesson.
Critically, much of the work centers on teachers deciding which student ideas they want to surface and in what order.
Each piece this week comes back to the same idea Kleist had long before we did: sometimes we figure out what we think by saying it out loud.
Try this: Before students start their next piece of writing, pair them up for five minutes of question-only coaching.
Those differences offer tremendous insight into where the lesson landed, and where you might go next.
